title: Attainment Setting and the Wrong Argument
author: Becky Allen
summary: Allen argues the decades-long UK debate over ability setting versus mixed-attainment teaching in maths has been fought on the wrong terrain. New evidence, she says, resolves the old moral argument cleanly: setting helps the strongest pupils and does not appear to be the engine of inequality the 'symbolic violence' critique long claimed, since disadvantaged students make similar progress and report similar self-confidence under either arrangement. But that resolution exposes a bigger, buried question -- why does neither setting nor mixed-attainment teaching meaningfully help low-attaining maths pupils? Her answer is structural: mathematics is a strongly hierarchical subject, so any whole-class explanation has to start somewhere, and mastery pedagogy has made this pre-existing constraint more visible rather than creating it. The real insight, she argues, is that a 'low set' is not a coherent teaching unit the way a top set is -- it bundles together students who are behind for entirely different reasons (dyscalculia, weak arithmetic fluency, attendance gaps, lost confidence), meaning setting policy alone can never address what are actually several distinct teaching problems wearing one label. She concludes the field should redirect two decades of setting-versus-mixed debate toward diagnosis and targeted intervention for these distinct subgroups.
points: New research settles the old moral argument: setting helps top-attaining pupils and does not damage disadvantaged students disproportionately -- FSM-eligible students make equivalent progress and report equivalent self-confidence whether set or mixed.

Allen locates the real constraint in the hierarchical structure of mathematics itself (you cannot teach Pythagoras before multiplication, area, and square roots), arguing mastery pedagogy made this pre-existing constraint more visible rather than inventing it.

Her key reframe: a low-attaining maths set is not one coherent teaching problem the way a top set is -- it bundles dyscalculic students, students with poor arithmetic fluency, students with attendance-driven gaps, and students who've lost confidence into a single label.

She estimates dyscalculia prevalence at 5-7% of the UK population, meaning a typical low-attaining class of 20-25 students may contain five or six students with a specific, identifiable mathematical learning difference requiring distinct intervention.

Allen's conclusion redirects the field's energy: neither setting nor mixed-attainment arrangement is a diagnosis-and-provision policy, so the next decade of research and practice should focus on specialized, targeted intervention rather than re-litigating the class-allocation question.
quotes: Setting is not, on this evidence, the engine of inequality the symbolic-violence argument has long claimed it to be.
You cannot teach a student Pythagoras’s theorem until they understand multiplication, area, square numbers and roots, and non-whole numbers.

This is why the case for setting in maths is strong. You can dislike setting and still grant the point: in a hierarchically organised subject, narrowing the prior-attainment range in a class makes whole-class instruction more tractable.
When you are weak at maths, the reasons you are weak can be wildly different from one student to the next. Estimates of dyscalculia prevalence in the UK sit at around five to seven per cent.
These are not four versions of the same student. They are four different teaching problems that happen to share the label of low maths attainment.

We have spent decades arguing about whether to set or not to set, and not enough time arguing about what would actually work for the students for whom both arrangements come out, on the evidence, roughly equivalently bad.
